single_permit.name: The single permit rules
single_permit.summary: If you work in an EU country on an ordinary work permit, these rights are yours. They were supposed to be in every EU country's own law by 21 May 2026. Some countries were late.
rights: A decision on a complete application within 90 days. But if they miss it, what happens is left to each country's own law — and the clock stops whenever a document is missing.
If your employer applies for you, the country must make sure your employer tells you how the application is going and how it ended.
You may change employer. A country can make you stay with your first employer for a while, but that period can never be longer than six months.
If your employer seriously breaks the terms of your job, you must be allowed to change employer even before that period ends.
Losing your job does not by itself cancel your permit — up to three months without work, or six months if you have held the permit more than two years. You must tell the authorities.
If the authorities have reason to believe you were working in badly exploitative conditions, that period must be extended by another three months.
If your permit runs out while your renewal is still being decided, you may stay.
Equal treatment with local workers on pay, working hours, dismissal, holidays, health and safety, joining a union and striking, training, and getting your qualifications recognised.
You can complain about your employer through someone else — a union or an organisation can act for you or alongside you, with your agreement. You do not have to put your own name to it.
Labour inspectors must be able to enter your workplace. If your employer also provides your housing, that includes your housing — but only if you agree to it.
Every country must publish, in a way reachable from outside the EU, what the conditions are and exactly which documents you need.
single_permit.fee_rule: Where your employer pays the fee for processing your permit application, your employer is not allowed to take that money back off you. Read it narrowly: it is about the government application fee, not about an agent's fee for finding you the job.
carved_out: People working on the basis of a visa rather than a permit
Posted workers, company transfers, self-employed people and seafarers
Possibly also anyone working six months or less, or admitted to study — each country may choose
single_permit.carved_out_warning: Seasonal work and au pair are named in the law itself as being outside these rules. That matters, because those are the cheapest and fastest-sounding routes. The quick door is the one with no lock on the inside.

talent_pool.name: The EU Talent Pool
talent_pool.summary: A free EU-wide website where people living outside the EU can put up a profile and see jobs in shortage occupations. It is law already. The website itself is not finished.
key_points: It is aimed exactly at people in your position: someone living outside the EU, old enough to work, who is not an EU citizen and is looking for a job in the EU.
You register by building a profile with the Europass profile builder.
Using it is free of charge for you. Employers and agencies using it are not allowed to charge you any fee or hidden cost for recruitment — not before, and not after you get the job.
The law names temporary work agencies, private employment agencies and labour market intermediaries. They are covered by that no-fee rule.
Countries join voluntarily, giving nine months' notice. So which countries are in it changes, and the list is published on the platform itself.
talent_pool.shortage_occupations_note: The law has a list of shortage occupations attached to it. It includes cooks, waiters, health care assistants, nurses, bricklayers, carpenters and joiners, roofers, plasterers, plumbers and pipe fitters, air conditioning and refrigeration mechanics, welders, sheet metal workers, motor vehicle mechanics, agricultural and industrial machinery mechanics, building electricians, butchers, bus and lorry drivers, and cleaners — as well as engineers, doctors, accountants and software developers. Those are, almost exactly, the trades you can train in on a German Ausbildung.
talent_pool.honest_caveat: The regulation itself gives no date for the website. The European Commission says it expects it to be fully working by the end of 2027. That is the Commission's expectation, not a deadline in the law. Do not plan around it, and be very careful of anyone who offers to register you on it for a fee.

long_term_residence.name: Five years is the real prize
long_term_residence.summary: In most EU countries, five years of legal residence lets you apply for long-term resident status, which is far more secure than a work permit tied to one employer and gives you rights in other EU countries too. Keep that number in mind when you read the sections below: a permit capped at four years, or a route written out of the five-year count, is a route that ends.

money.name: What is actually left to send home
money.summary: A wage on its own tells you almost nothing. Two people earning the same number of euros in two countries can send home very different amounts, and in some sectors the headline minimum wage does not apply at all. Here is how to work out the real figure, and what the law says can and cannot be taken off you.
steps: **Start with the gross monthly wage**, in writing, from the employer. Not a range, not "around", not what an agent tells you other people earn.

**Take off income tax and social insurance.** These are deducted before you ever see the money and they differ a lot between countries. The minimum wage figures on this page are gross — before any of this.

**Take off accommodation and food**, if your employer provides them. This is where the biggest surprises are. In Cyprus, for work that is covered by the minimum wage at all, the employer may cut the rate by 15% for meals and 10% for accommodation — and if you get both, the decree lets your wage fall to 75% of the full rate.
**Take off what you live on** — transport to work, phone, clothes, anything the employer does not provide.

**Take off the cost of sending the money.** Sending money home is not free. Compare two or three providers before you commit to one; transfers made through an app are generally cheaper than handing over cash.
**What is left is the real number.** Compare that against what you were asked to pay the agent, and against how many months it will take to earn it back.
money.pps_explainer: **The last column already includes the cost of living** — that is what it is for. Eurostat calls it the purchasing power standard: the same money restated for what it actually buys in that country, using that country's own prices. So you do not need to adjust it again for rent and food being cheaper in Sofia than in Munich. That has already been done. What it cannot tell you is what reaches Nepal, because what you send home is euros, and euros are not adjusted for Romanian prices when they arrive in Kathmandu. Read the middle column for what you could send, and the last one for how you would live while you are there.

accommodation_rights.heading: If your employer provides your housing
accommodation_rights.text: For **seasonal workers** in the EU there is a specific law about this, Directive 2014/36/EU. Where the employer arranges the accommodation, the rules require **rent that is not excessive**, they **prohibit the rent being deducted from your wages automatically**, and they make a **written rental contract compulsory**. The accommodation must meet an adequate standard for the whole of your stay, and the authorities are supposed to check it exists before you are admitted.
accommodation_rights.honest_caveat: Be realistic about enforcement. The European Commission reported in May 2026 that those three housing obligations were *"initially either not transposed, or only partially transposed, by eight Member States"*, and that stakeholders *"continue to report frequent breaches"* linked to weak monitoring and inspection. It also noted that rental contracts are *"often being provided in a language workers do not understand"*. Some countries have set concrete limits, such as capping rent at about one third of wages. Ask, in writing, what the rent will be and whether it comes out of your wage.

commission_on_agents.heading: The European Commission on who is charging you
commission_on_agents.text: In the same May 2026 report the Commission wrote that licensed intermediaries inside EU countries *"are often prohibited from charging workers"*, but that *"documented abuses persist, primarily, though not exclusively, in countries of origin, by unlicensed intermediaries during recruitment and admission, sometimes also during employment"*.
commission_on_agents.why_it_matters: That is the European Commission describing what happens in Nepal, in its own report to the European Parliament. The money is taken at this end, by people who are not licensed anywhere, for a service the destination country often forbids charging you for.

open: Deduction rates are measured at 50% of average earnings, the EU's standard low-wage benchmark, and not at the minimum wage. In countries where the minimum wage is well below that benchmark the real rate may be lower.

We are not publishing Eurostat's net earnings figures. For Malta, Portugal, Greece and Poland the published net does not equal gross minus tax and social contributions — in Portugal's case net comes out higher than gross — and we could not explain the difference. The tax and social contribution figures themselves are published directly and are what we have used.

Rent, food and transport in actual euros. There is no official source for what a low-paid migrant worker really spends, so we have not invented one. The purchasing power column is the closest honest substitute, and it uses an average national basket rather than yours.

The cost of sending money from each of these countries to Nepal. The World Bank publishes this corridor by corridor at remittanceprices.worldbank.org, but its site would not open for us. Its reported global average is around 6% of the amount sent, with digital transfers cheaper than cash — treat that as a prompt to compare providers, not as your figure.
Whether the countries on this page cap employer accommodation deductions, and at what level. Confirmed only for Cyprus.
money.deductions_explainer: How much is taken off before you are paid differs sharply from country to country. Romania takes about **41%** of gross in income tax and social insurance; Germany about 29%; Croatia 23%; Greece 19%; Malta 14%; and Cyprus and Portugal about **11%**. Those figures are for a single person without children on low pay, and they are the reason the second column is not simply a fixed fraction of the first.

straight_answer.heading: So which country actually leaves you better off?
straight_answer.text: This is a fair question to ask of any table, and for once the numbers point the same way on every measure. Compare Germany and Romania, the two ends of the page. Gross, it is **€2,343 against €825** — nearly three times as much. After deductions, **about €1,665 against about €490**, which is more than three times, because Romania takes **41%** off against Germany's 29%. And after the cost of living as well, **1,540 against 780** — still twice as much. In euros, after tax, and after prices, minimum-wage work in Germany leaves you better off than minimum-wage work in Romania. The same holds against Bulgaria, Croatia and the rest.
straight_answer.caveats_heading: Three things that number does not know about you
caveats: **The cost-of-living adjustment uses an ordinary national shopping basket** — one that includes things like buying a home, which you will not be doing. If your employer provides your housing and food, your real costs look nothing like the average, and in that case the euro column matters far more than the purchasing power one.
**The deduction rate is measured at a standard low-wage benchmark**, not at the minimum wage itself. Where tax rises in steps, your rate could be lower than the figure shown.

**It assumes you are paid the minimum wage.** In Cyprus the minimum wage does not cover agriculture, private households or trainees at all. Check which rate applies to the work you are actually being offered before you compare anything.

ausbildung_caveat.heading: How poor are the training years, really?
ausbildung_caveat.text:
This is where we got it wrong earlier and have corrected it, so read this part carefully.

Germany's minimum wage is €2,343 a month, and **an Ausbildung does not pay that** — training is not ordinary employment, so the minimum wage does not apply. The legal floor for a contract starting in 2026 is **€724** a month in the first year. But that is a floor, and most apprentices do considerably better: the average first-year allowance under collective agreements is **€1,117**, and nursing pays about **€1,491**.

That range changes the comparison completely. On the legal minimum an apprentice keeps about €570, and what that buys in Germany — about **525** — is less than a minimum-wage worker gets in any country on this page. On the typical allowance they keep about €880, worth about **815**, which is a little ahead of Bulgaria and Romania. On a nursing contract they keep about €1,170, worth about **1,080** — level with Cyprus and ahead of Croatia, Greece and Malta.
ausbildung_caveat.conclusion:
**So the honest answer depends entirely on the trade and the employer, and the gap between the best and worst is enormous** — from about €490 a month in the hand as a hairdressing apprentice to about €1,170 in nursing. That is not a detail to settle after you arrive. It is the single biggest financial decision in the whole plan, and it is made when you choose which training place to accept.

Two things remain true whichever trade you pick. The training years pay less than ordinary work in Germany, often much less — so **make sure your family understands that the money starts later**, and do not borrow against a remittance that will not arrive for three years. And the case for an Ausbildung was never the money during training. It is that you finish holding a qualification recognised across Europe and named on the EU's own shortage list, with German work at around €1,665 a month net then open to you and considerably better than that in a skilled trade. That is a bet on what happens afterwards. It is a reasonable bet. It is still a bet.
ausbildung_caveat.arithmetic_note: How these were worked out. Income tax is zero at almost every Ausbildung wage: on €1,117 a month, taxable income after the deductible social insurance and the standard allowances comes to roughly €9,500 a year, well under the German basic tax-free allowance. Only nursing goes above it, and only by about €8 a month. So the deduction that matters is social insurance — the employee half of pension 9.3%, unemployment 1.3%, health 7.3% plus about half the supplementary rate, and care 1.8%, with 0.6% more for someone childless over 23. That is roughly 21%. Apprentices are excluded from the reduced-contribution band for low earners and pay the full share from the first euro. Net figures are gross less 21%, rounded to €5. The gross figures are official; the net figures are our arithmetic.

money.table_note: The first column is the **gross** statutory minimum wage in force on 1 July 2026 — the figure an employer or an agent will quote you. The second is **roughly what is left** after income tax and your own social insurance. The third is what that remaining money **actually buys** in that country, because €800 in Sofia and €800 in Valletta are not the same amount of money.

net_method.heading: How we worked out the second column, and why you should treat it as rough
net_method.text: **There is no official table of net minimum wages in Europe.** Eurostat publishes the gross minimum wage, and separately it publishes how much income tax and social insurance comes off a low-paid single worker. We have multiplied the two. That is our arithmetic, not a published figure, which is why every number in that column is rounded to the nearest €5.
caveats: The deduction rate is measured at a standard EU low-wage benchmark rather than at the minimum wage exactly. In Croatia, Poland and Germany those two are almost the same, so the figure is close. In Cyprus and Malta the minimum wage sits well below the benchmark.
Where they differ, the error runs **in your favour** — income tax allowances mean you would usually pay a little less than shown, so the real amount kept is the same or slightly more, never less.
In Cyprus and Portugal no income tax is paid at this level at all, so only social insurance comes off and those two figures are solid.
None of this includes anything your employer takes for food or housing. That comes off afterwards, and in Cyprus it can be a further 25%.

what_changes.heading: Why this matters more than it looks
what_changes.text: Switching from gross to net does not just shrink every number by the same amount — it **changes the order**. On gross pay Poland looks like the second best country on this page. Once deductions come off it is sixth. Romania keeps about 59% of gross while Portugal and Cyprus keep about 89%, so Romania's €825 and Portugal's €1,073 are much further apart in reality than they look on paper. If you are comparing offers, compare the second column, and ask every employer what the figure is after deductions.

ausbildung_wages.heading: What an Ausbildung actually pays, by trade
ausbildung_wages.intro: The €724 figure above is the **legal floor**, not the normal rate. Most employers are bound by a collective agreement and pay well above it. These are the average collectively agreed allowances for the **first training year**, from the German federal vocational training institute's own figures, reference date 1 October 2025 — except nursing, which is paid under a different agreement and is the best-paid route of all.
ausbildung_wages.average_note: Across all trades the average first-year allowance is **€1,117**, and **€1,209** averaged over all training years. So the typical apprentice gets roughly half as much again as the legal minimum.

rows.note: TVAöD-Pflege from 1 May 2026. Church employers are similar: Caritas around €1,502 from February 2026. State and university hospitals under TVA-L pay about €1,440. The best-paid route on this page — if the employer is bound by one of these agreements.

rows.name: Nursing — private employer, not tariff-bound
rows.note: **No figure, because there is no floor.** See the section below. A private provider may pay whatever counts as "appropriate", and we could not find reliable published figures for what they actually pay.

rows.note: Rises to €1,472 by the fourth year. Note the length: this one runs **42 months**, three and a half years, not three.

rows.name: Pipeline construction (Rohrleitungsbauer/-in)
rows.note: Rises to €1,501 by the third year — one of the steepest climbs of any trade here.

rows.name: Railway track laying (Gleisbauer/-in)
rows.note: Rises to €1,448 by the third year.

rows.name: Road building (Straßenbauer/-in)
rows.note: Rises to €1,508 by the third year. Crafts firms pay almost the same as industry in this trade, unusually.

rows.name: Car mechanic, crafts (Kfz-Mechatroniker/-in)
rows.note: The same job in industry rather than a crafts firm averages €1,202.

rows.name: Groundworks (Tiefbaufacharbeiter/-in)
rows.note: A two-year qualification rather than three, rising to €1,260 in the second year. It can be built on afterwards with a further year to a full trade.

rows.name: Electrician, crafts (Elektroniker/-in, all specialisms)
rows.note: The same job in industry averages €1,227 — nearly €250 a month more.

rows.name: Refrigeration and air conditioning (Mechatroniker/-in für Kältetechnik)
rows.note: Also called Mechatroniker, but a crafts qualification and a very different rate — €933 against €1,224. It is on the EU shortage occupation list.

rows.name: Hairdresser (Friseur/-in)
rows.note: Below the statutory minimum, and lawfully so: an employer bound by a collective agreement may follow that agreement even where it pays less.

ausbildung_wages.craft_vs_industry: **Where you train changes the pay as much as what you train in.** The same qualification pays very differently in a small crafts firm (*Handwerk*) and in an industrial or commercial company (*Industrie und Handel*). A car mechanic averages €1,090 in a crafts firm and €1,202 in industry; an electrician €979 against €1,227 — nearly €250 a month for the same trade. Ask which agreement the employer is bound by before you sign.
ausbildung_wages.floor_warning: **A collective agreement may legally pay less than the statutory minimum.** Hairdressing averages €623 in the first year, below the €724 floor, and that is lawful where the employer is bound by the agreement. An employer who is *not* bound by one may pay up to 20% below the regional rate for the trade. So the €724 is not a guarantee either.
ausbildung_wages.trades_caveat: **We do not have statistics on which trades applicants from Nepal actually choose.** Nepal's labour data records destination countries, not training occupations. The trades above were chosen because they appear on the EU's own shortage occupation list, because they come up most often in what readers write to us, and — for mechatronics in particular — because it is reported to us as one of the most sought-after choices among young people in Nepal. That is an observation, not a measurement. If you have been offered something not on this list, [tell us](/contact/) and we will look it up.

construction_note.heading: A note on the building trades, and on Tiefbau in particular
construction_note.text:
Construction is worth looking at closely, for three reasons that have nothing to do with anyone's sales pitch.

**The pay starts around the average and then climbs steeply.** A road builder starts at €1,091 and is on **€1,508** by the third year; a bricklayer €1,079 rising to €1,533; pipeline construction €1,162 rising to €1,501. Across all trades in Germany the third-year average is €1,297, so the building trades finish roughly €200 a month ahead of it. If you are comparing offers, compare the third year as well as the first.

**It is a sector that already employs people from outside Germany.** The construction industry's own federation reports that the share of foreign workers in the main construction trades rose from 8% in 2009 to **25% in 2025**, and in above-ground building trades to **36%**. You would not be unusual there.

**Within construction, groundworks and civil engineering is the part that grew.** In 2024, when the sector shed staff overall, employment rose in Tiefbau and fell in Hochbau.
construction_note.shortage_honesty: **But be careful with the word "shortage".** It is true that German construction has had a long-running skills problem, and surveys of civil engineering firms report high rates of unfilled posts. It is also true that the pressure has eased: in the industry federation's own summary the assessment has *"etwas entspannt"* — relaxed somewhat — with **54%** of construction firms naming skills shortage as a business risk in early summer 2026, against **81%** at the start of 2019. Employment in the main construction trades rose to 923,000 in 2025 and is expected to reach 933,000 in 2026. A shortage that is easing is still a shortage, but it is not the emergency it is sometimes described as, and the strongest shortage figures you will see quoted are usually about **civil engineers and site managers** — university-level jobs — rather than about apprentices.
construction_note.dropout_warning: **The figure nobody quotes at you.** According to the Federal Statistical Office, **40% of training contracts in building and civil engineering are ended early.** That is the highest-risk number on this page and you should know it before you sign a three-year contract in this sector. One important caveat: in German statistics an "early termination" is not the same as giving up — a large share of those people move to another employer or another trade and finish their training elsewhere. But it tells you that building sites are physically hard, often outdoors in a German winter, and that a lot of people who start do not finish where they started.

nursing_note.heading: Nursing: the one trade with no minimum wage of its own
nursing_note.lede: Nursing is the best-paid training route on this page and the one most often suggested to people from Nepal. It is also the only one on this page where **the statutory minimum training allowance does not apply at all.** If you take one thing from this page about nursing, take this.
nursing_note.why: Every other trade here is trained under the Vocational Training Act, which sets a legal floor — €724 a month for a contract starting in 2026. Nursing is trained under a different law, the **Pflegeberufegesetz**. Its § 19 says only that the employer must pay *"eine angemessene Ausbildungsvergütung"* — an appropriate training allowance. **The statute names no amount.** There is no €724 floor in nursing. There is no figure at all.
what_this_means: **A public hospital or a council-run provider** pays under TVAöD-Pflege: about **€1,491** a month in the first year from 1 May 2026, rising to about €1,653 by the third year.

**A church provider** — Caritas or Diakonie, which between them run a very large share of German care — pays under its own rules, broadly similar. Caritas is reported at about **€1,502** from February 2026.
**A state or university hospital** pays under TVA-L, about **€1,440**.

**A private provider that is not bound by any agreement** sets its own figure. It must be "appropriate", and nothing more precise than that. We could not find reliable published figures for what private providers actually pay trainees, which is itself worth knowing.
nursing_note.leverage: **One fact worth having in that conversation.** Nursing training allowances are not paid out of the employer's own pocket in the way other trades are. They are refinanced through a state-level fund (*Landesfonds*) to which all care providers contribute, and which reimburses the cost of the training allowance. So an employer who says they cannot afford to pay more is describing a choice, not a constraint. Ask which collective agreement, if any, the contract follows, and ask before you sign.

sachbezug.heading: And the part that can take most of it away again
sachbezug.text: § 19(2) of the same law allows **board and lodging to be set off against your allowance**, at official national values, **if — and only if — your training contract says so**. The 2026 values are **€345 a month for food** and **€285 for accommodation**, so **€630** for both. The law caps the total offset at **75% of your gross allowance**.
sachbezug.worked: What that does in practice: on a tariff allowance of €1,491 gross, social insurance takes roughly €313, and full board and lodging can take a further €630 — leaving about **€550 in cash** rather than about €1,170. That is not necessarily a worse deal, because you are not then paying rent or buying food. But it is a completely different number, and it is the one that reaches your family. Find out which of the two your offer is.
sachbezug.protection: Two protections in the same provision are worth knowing. The offset is only lawful **if it is agreed in the training contract** — it cannot be introduced afterwards. And if you cannot take the board or lodging for a legitimate reason, the employer must **pay you its value in cash instead**. There is also a rule that work beyond your agreed training hours is only exceptionally permitted and must be separately paid or given back as time off.

mechatroniker_note.heading: If somebody has told you to do "Mechatroniker"
mechatroniker_note.text:
It is a popular choice and a well-paid one, but **"Mechatroniker" is not one qualification — it is at least six**, and what you are paid depends on which one you sign for:

- **Mechatroniker/-in** (industry) — **€1,224** in the first year, rising to €1,472 in the fourth
- **Kraftfahrzeugmechatroniker/-in**, vehicles — **€1,202** in industry, **€1,090** in a crafts firm
- **Land- und Baumaschinenmechatroniker/-in**, agricultural and construction machinery — **€1,121** in industry, **€930** in a crafts firm
- **Zweiradmechatroniker/-in**, motorcycles and bicycles — €1,110 in industry, €1,050 in crafts
- **Mechatroniker/-in für Kältetechnik**, refrigeration and air conditioning — **€933**, and on the EU shortage list
- **Rollladen- und Sonnenschutzmechatroniker/-in**, shutters and sun protection — €946

That is a spread of nearly **€300 a month in the first year** between jobs with almost the same name, and the gap widens over the training. Three of them also run **42 months rather than 36** — three and a half years, which is worth knowing when you are planning.
mechatroniker_note.advice: **So the question to ask is not "is this Mechatroniker?" but "which Mechatroniker, and is the employer in industry or in the crafts?"** Get the exact German job title and the chamber — IHK for industry, HWK for crafts — written into the contract, and check it against the figures above before you sign.

money.ausbildung_rows_footnote: Not minimum wages. The first is the statutory minimum training allowance for a contract starting in 2026; the second is the average collectively agreed first-year allowance across all trades; the third is nursing. See the breakdown by trade below.

language.name: Language — the gate that rules Germany out for a lot of people
language.lede: Almost every page on this site assumes you will learn German. For a great many people that assumption is wrong, and nobody says so. If languages are hard for you, that is not a character failure and it is not something to push through — it is a fact to plan around, and it changes which countries are realistic.

what_b1_means.heading: What B1 German actually means
what_b1_means.text:
B1 is not conversational German. It is the level at which you can follow the main points of clear, standard speech about familiar everyday things, handle most situations that come up, write simple connected text, and give short reasons for an opinion. It is a real working level and it takes real time.

The Goethe-Institut's own estimate is **260 to 490 guided hours** to reach B1 from nothing. A guided hour is 45 minutes of taught class — homework and self-study are on top. At ten hours of class a week that is **six months to a year**, if nothing goes wrong.
what_b1_means.the_catch: **And that estimate is not written for you.** Those hour ranges assume a learner whose first language is a European one. Nepali is not. German grammar — three genders, four cases, verbs at the end — has no equivalent you can lean on, and the vocabulary shares almost no roots. Nobody we can find publishes an honest figure for a Nepali first-language learner, so we will not invent one. Assume the Goethe range is a **floor**, not an estimate.
what_b1_means.plus_the_queue: Then add the exam. In Nepal the hard part is often not learning the German but getting a seat in the test, and the certificate must be **no older than six months** when you apply. [That bottleneck has its own page](/exam-slots/), and it is the part most people are not warned about.

two_gates.heading: Two different gates, and most people only hear about one
two_gates.text: Every country below has two language questions, and they have very different answers. The first decides whether you can go at all. The second decides whether what you are going to leads anywhere permanent. A country can be wide open on one and shut on the other.

if_german_is_not_realistic.heading: If German is honestly not going to happen
if_german_is_not_realistic.text:
Then say so early, to yourself and to anybody taking your money. A year of lessons you will not pass is the most expensive thing on this page — more than most agents charge, and it costs you the year as well.

What is actually open without a language certificate: **Malta**, where English is an official language and the working language of business; **Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia, Portugal and Greece**, none of which ask for anything to let you in; and the **UK seasonal route**, six months in horticulture.
if_german_is_not_realistic.the_trade:
**But look at what you are trading.** The countries with no language gate are, almost exactly, the countries with no qualification at the end, permits tied to one employer, and the weakest rights on this page. The one route that ends with something that belongs to you — a qualification recognised across Europe — is the one that asks for B1 German first. That is not a coincidence. The language requirement is part of what makes the destination worth reaching.

So the honest choice is not "easy country or hard country". It is: **spend the year on German and get a qualification, or skip the year and get a job.** Both are legitimate. Only one of them is usually explained to you.
if_german_is_not_realistic.worth_knowing: One more thing worth knowing before you decide German is impossible. You do not need B1 to **start applying** — you can look for a training place at a lower level, and employers in some trades will take someone who is still learning. What you need B1 for is the **visa**. And some vocational schools want B2 rather than B1 once you are there. [The application pages explain how that sequence works](/apply/).

sources.label: Goethe-Institut's cumulative guided-learning-hour estimates for German (A1 60–150, A2 150–260, B1 260–490, B2 450–600), and the CEFR's own plain description of what a B1 speaker can do. Cyprus long-term residence: Greek at A2 plus an examination on the political and social reality of Cyprus. From a Cypriot law firm — the Migration Department's own page lists the procedure and fees but does not spell out the examinations.

Romania's language test at five years and Portugal's Portuguese requirements: EU Immigration Portal country pages, last updated 1 April 2025. Croatia's A1.1 requirement from June 2027: reporting on the June 2026 amendments to the Foreigners Act.

countries.name: Germany
countries.headline: The only route in Europe we have found that pays you a wage from the first month and ends with a qualification — and the one almost nobody from Nepal actually gets.

qualification.note: A state-recognised German vocational qualification, normally three years.

countries.sectors: All trades. On the day we checked, the federal employment agency was advertising 165,002 training places.

pay.text: At least €1,090 a month in the first training year, rising each year. That figure is from one German chamber's own Nepal programme terms, marked August 2026.

family.text: Possible for a husband, wife or children, but the marriage must already exist before your permit is issued — that cannot be fixed afterwards. There are income and housing tests. See our family page.

If your employer gets you a Vorabzustimmung, the embassy has told us in writing it will give you an appointment inside three weeks.

The Opportunity Card sold as the easy way in. It needs either a qualification already recognised in Germany, or six points plus a two-year qualification and German A1 or English B2 — and proof of money, which for a blocked account is €13,104. That is more than most agents charge.

countries.headline: A real apprenticeship route that you can apply for from Nepal — and a wage requirement that may put it out of reach.

countries.name: Cyprus
countries.headline: The second biggest destination, and the one where nearly two thirds of the Nepalis going are women. Read the part about five years carefully.

Seasonal work, four months at a time, extendable by another four

But the Migration Department expressly leaves out of that count: students and people living in Cyprus for vocational training; people there only temporarily, giving unpaid domestic workers and seasonal workers as its examples; and anyone whose permit has been officially restricted. Ordinary employment permits are also capped — the EU portal says four years for most jobs, with agriculture, domestic work and some other jobs on different terms. Being told the work leads to settlement. For seasonal work and for anyone there on a restricted permit, it is written out of the five-year count.

countries.name: Hungary
countries.headline: Closed to Nepali citizens. Not difficult — not permitted.
countries.brief: Hungary publishes a list of countries whose citizens may hold a work residence permit. The list, set by Government Decree 450/2024, has three countries on it: Georgia, Armenia and the Philippines. Nepal is not on it, and is not on the separate lists for guest workers or for the National Card either. New guest worker permits stopped entirely in June 2026. Even for people who do qualify, family reunification is not allowed, except for a child born in Hungary. If someone offers you a Hungarian work visa, this is the thing to show them.
open: The June 2026 closure date for new guest worker permits comes from secondary reporting. The country list itself we read on the Hungarian immigration authority's own site.

countries.name: Poland
countries.headline: Open, but the work visa is decided in New Delhi — not Kathmandu.
countries.brief: Poland changed its rules on 1 June 2025: all work permit applications are now electronic, the labour market test was abolished, and your signed employment contract must be uploaded before you start work. Permit fees changed on 1 December 2025. Poland has no embassy in Nepal. Long-stay work visas are handled by the Polish Embassy in New Delhi, which takes applications on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday at 10:00 and decides within fifteen days. Switzerland's embassy in Kathmandu represents Poland — but only for short-stay Schengen visas, not for work. This is the single most common misunderstanding we have found.

countries.name: Czechia
countries.headline: Technically open. In practice rationed by a yearly quota in New Delhi.
countries.brief: The Czech Embassy in New Delhi covers India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and the Maldives — six countries sharing a yearly quota of 1,560 employee cards. Since October 2025 it accepts employee card applications only through one of the Czech government's economic migration programmes, and refuses requests for ad-hoc appointments. Applicants inside a programme are given an appointment; nobody can sell you one. The Czech honorary consulate in Kathmandu says appointments for Nepali and Bangladeshi citizens are allocated only by telephone line, though that page looks old.
open: Whether Nepali citizens are eligible for the Qualified Worker Programme at all. We could not establish this, and it is the question that decides whether Czechia is a route for you or not.

countries.name: Italy
countries.headline: The biggest quota in Europe, a fixed application day, and a scam built around it.
countries.brief: Italy's three-year decree for 2026 to 2028 allows 497,550 workers, about 164,850 a year. Only an Italian employer can apply, and only on a fixed "click day" — 12 January for seasonal agriculture, 9 February for seasonal tourism, 16 February for workers from countries with cooperation agreements, and 18 February for everyone else. Some quotas are reserved for countries that have migration agreements with Italy. Nepal is not on that list. A 2024 report on Italy's system found at least 139 identified victims of people posing as agents, taking money for click-day applications and disappearing. If you are asked to pay for an Italian click-day application, that is the scam.

single_permit.note: Seasonal work is carved out; ordinary work is not.

open: The list of countries with cooperation agreements: one source names eight, another names thirty-one. Nepal is on neither, which is the part that matters.

countries.name: Serbia
countries.headline: Not in the EU and not in Schengen, so none of the EU rights above apply.
countries.brief: Nearly 2,900 Nepalis took labour approvals for Serbia in 2025/26. Nepali citizens always need a visa: a long-stay D visa, then a combined residence and work permit issued for up to three years. Because Serbia is outside the EU, none of the single permit rights described above reach you there, and Serbian time does not count towards EU long-term residence. Serbia is also a known fraud route: nineteen Nepalis were reported to have been defrauded of Rs 70 lakh in a Serbian work visa scam run from Delhi.

countries.name: Lithuania
countries.headline: Quota-limited, and once the quota is gone the wage bar is high.
countries.brief: Lithuania set a quota of 24,706 for 2026 and publishes a shortage list of about 110 occupations, updated each January; jobs on it skip the local advertising requirement. Once the yearly quota is used up, a permit is still possible but the employer must pay at least 1.2 times the average national wage, which for 2026 is about €2,893.68 a month. All of this is secondary reporting — we have not read the Lithuanian migration department's own pages.
open: Everything in this entry. Verify at the Lithuanian migration department before relying on it.

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.headline: Possible, and the Kathmandu confusion applies here too.
countries.brief: Slovakia's long-stay D visa now runs 120 days, to give you time to reach Slovakia and attend the compulsory Foreign Police appointment after arrival. Switzerland's embassy in Kathmandu represents Slovakia — but for short-stay Schengen visas only, not for work. We have done little research on Slovakia.
open: Almost everything. Treat this entry as a pointer, not as information.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.headline: Open on paper, but most of the jobs Nepalis are offered in Europe are on the ineligible list.
countries.brief: A General Employment Permit needs a job paying at least €36,605 a year from 1 March 2026, with lower figures for healthcare assistants and home carers (€32,691). The permit is only for jobs not on the Ineligible List of Occupations, which rules out most hospitality and retail below management level, general clerical work, most agricultural and food processing operative jobs, domestic work, and most transport and logistics below a skill threshold. In practice that excludes most of what is advertised to Nepali workers.

single_permit.note: Ireland is not bound by the EU single permit rules.

open: The 2026 figures come from Citizens Information, an Irish state body, rather than from the department itself.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.headline: One route genuinely open — six months of farm work, with no family and no settlement.
countries.brief: The Seasonal Worker visa allows up to six months in horticulture, or work in poultry from 2 October to 31 December. You need a licensed scheme operator as your sponsor, the application fee is £340, you must show personal savings, and in the Home Office's own words: "You cannot bring family members with you." It leads to no settlement. The Skilled Worker route is a different matter: the skill level is now degree level and the general salary floor is around £41,700, and the care worker route closed to new applicants from overseas on 22 July 2025. A proposal to extend settlement from five years to ten was in the 2025 immigration white paper but, as of late September 2026, had not become law — treat it as a proposal, not a rule.
countries.health_note: Nepal is on the UK's amber list for health and care recruitment. That means recruitment is only allowed under the terms of the government-to-government agreement in place, which currently covers one NHS trust and is still a pilot. But the code says it does not stop individuals "independently applying ... of their own accord and without being targeted by a third party." The restriction binds recruiters, not you — exactly as it does in Germany.

single_permit.note: The UK is not in the EU.

open: The Skilled Worker figures and the care worker closure date come from immigration law sources, not from gov.uk directly.
The ten-year settlement proposal. It is a proposal. We will not state it as the rule.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.headline: A quota of 8,500 for the whole world, and only for qualified people.
countries.brief: For 2026 Switzerland allows at most 8,500 third-country workers — 4,500 longer permits and 4,000 short-stay ones. Admission is limited to managers, specialists and other qualified workers where it serves Swiss economic interest, and Swiss and EU candidates come first. Switzerland does have an embassy in Kathmandu, and it handles short-stay Schengen visas for Liechtenstein, Poland, Belgium, Slovakia and Latvia as well. That is short-stay only. It is not a work visa service for any of those countries.

countries.name: Sweden, Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark and the rest
countries.headline: Statistically almost nobody, and for a reason.
countries.brief: In 2025/26 the Netherlands took 62 Nepali labour approvals, Belgium 20 and Sweden 9. These countries have high salary floors and expect degree-level qualifications, and none of them has a route for a young person with no qualification and no money. France and Spain took 146 each. We have not researched them in detail because the numbers suggest no realistic route — not because a route is impossible. If you have been offered work in one of these countries, that is not automatically a scam, but it is unusual enough to check very carefully.

au_pair.intro: Au pair is suggested often in Nepal, usually when the German exam queue starts to look impossible. One thing to know before you read further: the EU single permit law names au pairs as being outside its protections. None of the rights listed above — the six-month limit on being tied to one employer, the protection if you lose your job, the right to complain through someone else — reach an au pair in the EU.

countries.name: Norway
countries.text: The scheme was abolished with effect from 15 March 2024. If you are being offered an au pair placement in Norway, there is no permit for it. This is the most useful fact on this list, because it is still being advertised.
open: Confirmed by three independent reports that agree. We could not read Norway's own immigration pages, which block automated access.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.text: Age 18 and not yet 30. You must be able to manage in Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, English or German. Pocket money of at least DKK 5,250 a month at 2026 rates. Between 18 and 30 hours of work a week, three to five hours a day, at most six days a week, with at least a day and a half off plus Danish public holidays. Maximum stay two years. The host family must include a child under 18 and at least one parent must be a Danish or EU citizen, or a long-term resident with strong Danish ties. The application fee is DKK 4,305, and the host family pays DKK 20,900 towards your Danish classes if you are a first-time applicant. Processing normally takes three months.

sources.label: nyidanmark.dk, Danish Agency for International Recruitment and Integration — au pair. Page last updated 26 June 2026.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.text: One year, and it cannot be extended. Age 18 to 25 at application. Only an au pair agency recognised by the Dutch immigration service can apply for you — you cannot apply yourself. Light housekeeping only, at most eight hours a day and 30 hours a week, at the host family's registered address. You must be unmarried, have no children, not be related to the host family, not have worked for them before anywhere, and not have held a Dutch residence permit before. The fee is €423. It leads to nothing further.

other_routes.name: Study
other_routes.text: Public universities in Germany charge no tuition fees, and Poland and Czechia offer programmes taught in English. Erasmus Mundus scholarships are fully funded and genuinely open — 33 Nepali students were awarded them for master's study, according to the EU delegation in Nepal. We have not researched study routes properly and are not going to give you figures we have not checked.

other_routes.name: Seasonal work, as a category
other_routes.text: Across the UK, Bulgaria, Italy, Romania and Cyprus the shape is the same: short, tied to one employer, no qualification at the end, usually no family, and no path to staying. And in the EU it is specifically excluded from the single permit protections. It is the fastest route and the one with the least protection.

other_routes.name: Nepal's bilateral labour agreements
other_routes.text: Nepal has sent draft labour agreements to a number of European countries — reports differ on whether it is eleven or sixteen. A draft sent is not an agreement signed, and an agreement signed is not an open application. Germany's own employment agency told us in writing that for Germany "ein offenes oder direktes Bewerbungsverfahren für Einzelpersonen über die ZAV existiert derzeit jedoch nicht" — there is no open or direct application procedure for individuals. Assume the same elsewhere until a government page says otherwise.

other_routes.name: "Free visa, free ticket"
other_routes.text: This covers seven Gulf destinations. It has never covered Germany or any part of Europe.

scam_patterns.check: For work visas, usually it is not. Several countries are represented in Kathmandu for short-stay Schengen visas only — Switzerland's embassy covers Liechtenstein, Poland, Belgium, Slovakia and Latvia that way, and Sweden's applications go via VFS Global in Kathmandu to the embassy in New Delhi, which also handles Denmark and Estonia. The work or training visa is a different, national visa, and for most countries it is decided in New Delhi. That means an Indian visa, travel and a queue that nobody mentions when quoting you a fee. Ask which city will decide your visa, and ask for it in writing.

Nobody can sell you a place in a queue. Czech programme applicants are given their appointment by the consulate. Polish work visa slots belong to the embassy. German appointments in Kathmandu come from a waiting list. If someone is charging you for an appointment, ask them to show you the government page that says appointments can be bought.

scam_patterns.pattern: An "approved" permit or job offer you cannot verify.
scam_patterns.check: Ask which government system holds it and what its reference number is. In Romania, since May 2026, nothing can even be started outside WorkinRomania.gov.ro. In Italy, only an Italian employer can apply, and only on a fixed day of the year.

scam_patterns.pattern: A route that has been closed.
scam_patterns.check: Portugal's tourist-then-regularise route ended permanently on 31 December 2025. Norway's au pair scheme ended on 15 March 2024. Hungary's work permits are not open to Nepali citizens at all. Austria has no apprenticeship visa and never has had one. All four are still being sold.

scam_patterns.pattern: "There is a government-to-government agreement, so you can apply."
scam_patterns.check: Ask where the application form is. For Germany the employment agency has told us there is no individual application route. A chamber of commerce agreement, like the one in Piraeus, is not a government programme at all.

scam_patterns.pattern: A fee that is not itemised.
scam_patterns.check: Ask for it split: lessons, exam fees, translation and certification, document handling, travel. Ask what happens to your money if the visa is refused, and get the answer in writing before you pay. In Nepal, licensed consultancies must publish their fees and may not take cash.
